Dynamic sparsity in tree-structured feed-forward layers at scale

Reza Sedghi Affiliation: CITEC, Bielefeld University, Germany Correspondence to: reza.sedghi@uni-bielefeld.de    Robin Schiewer Affiliation: CITEC, Bielefeld University, Germany Correspondence to: robin.schiewer@uni-bielefeld.de    Anand Subramoney Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Royal Holloway, University of London, UK Correspondence to: anand.subramoney@rhul.ac.uk    David Kappel Affiliation: CITEC, Bielefeld University, Germany Correspondence to: david.kappel@uni-bielefeld.de
Abstract

At typical context lengths, the feed-forward MLP block accounts for a large share of a transformer’s compute budget, motivating sparse alternatives to dense MLP blocks. We study sparse, tree-structured feed-forward layers as drop-in replacements for MLP blocks in deep transformer architectures, enabling conditional computation via hard hierarchical routing without a separate router network. We demonstrate for the first time that this form of tree-structured conditional sparsity can be applied for autoregressive language modeling and downstream question answering, including zero- and few-shot settings, and its scalability beyond 1B parameters. Despite activating fewer than 5% of the feed-forward block’s units per token, our models match dense baselines under controlled training and fine-tuning protocols. We further analyze training dynamics and identify an emergent auto-pruning effect: the interaction of hard routing with asymmetric nonlinearities progressively deactivates unused paths, yielding partial conversion of dynamic routing into static structural sparsity. We show that simple architectural choices can modulate this behavior and recover balanced trees without auxiliary losses. Overall, our work demonstrates that tree-structured feed-forward layers provide a scalable and controllable mechanism for sparsifying large transformer models.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Feed-forward (FF) or MLP blocks account for a dominant fraction of parameters and computation in modern transformer architectures, particularly in large language models (LLMs). As models scale to billions of parameters, the cost of dense FF blocks has become a primary bottleneck, motivating extensive research into sparse alternatives. Among these, mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have emerged as a prominent approach to exploit dynamic sparsity by activating only a subset of parameters per token (Mu and Lin, 2025) (see Fig. 1a,b). However, practical MoE systems typically rely on learned routing networks, auxiliary load-balancing losses, and specialized training and inference infrastructure (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022; Gale et al., 2023).

Tree-structured conditional computation offers a different sparsification mechanism, that organizes computation hierarchically, such that each input activates a single root-to-leaf path in a binary tree. This induces predictable and structured sparsity: routing decisions at each level deterministically select a subtree, allowing entire paths to be skipped without a separate router module or expert aggregation. This enables high levels of sparsity with minimal architectural overhead. Fast Feedforward (FFF) layers (Belcák and Wattenhofer, 2023b; Belcák and Wattenhofer, 2023a) instantiated this idea by replacing dense FF blocks by a sequence of hard binary routing decisions, activating only a small number of nodes while all other parameters remain inactive. As a result, FFF layers can achieve levels of dynamic sparsity exceeding 99%99\%. However, apart from encoder-style BERT models for classification with ca. 300M parameters (Belcák and Wattenhofer, 2023a), the capabilities and limitations of tree-structured conditional computation remains largely unexplored compared to widely used MoEs.

In this work, we address these open questions through a systematic empirical and analytical study of FFF layers in GPT-style transformers. We evaluate models trained from scratch and via fine-tuning across a wide range of scales, including models with over a billion parameters, and assess performance on language modeling as well as zero- and few-shot downstream benchmarks. Across these settings, we show that FFF-based models closely match dense feed-forward baselines while operating in highly sparse computational regimes. Beyond scalability and performance, we discover a new emergent auto-pruning effect, in which the interaction between hard routing decisions and asymmetric nonlinearities progressively deactivates entire tree paths during training. This process partially converts dynamic, input-dependent routing into stable structural sparsity, yielding additional computational savings without explicit pruning criteria or auxiliary regularization. We further show that this behavior is not incidental but can be modulated through simple architectural choices.

Overall, our results demonstrate that tree-structured feed-forward layers constitute a practical and scalable alternative to dense FF blocks and MoE architectures.

Contributions.

This work provides the first systematic investigation of hard-routed tree-structured feed-forward layers in large transformer models. Our contributions are: (i) we demonstrate, for the first time, that FFF layers scale to billion-parameter autoregressive language models while maintaining performance comparable to dense feed-forward baselines; (ii) we identify and analyze an emergent auto-pruning mechanism that converts dynamic tree routing into stable structural sparsity during training; (iii) we show that routing imbalance and tree utilization can be controlled through simple architectural choices, without auxiliary losses or explicit expert-balancing mechanisms; and (iv) we provide the first layer-level runtime benchmarks that quantify its efficiency trade-offs.

2 Related Work

Sparse and conditional computation has been widely studied as a means to scale neural networks efficiently. Early work on hierarchical mixtures of experts (HMEs) introduced tree-structured gating mechanisms to enable conditional execution in deep models (Jordan and Jacobs, 1993). More recent variants explore hierarchical or dynamic expert routing within transformer architectures (Zhao et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022). Differentiable decision-tree layers have been proposed as neural network components that combine tree ensembles with end-to-end training (Hazimeh et al., 2020), but these architectures are typically evaluated on vision or tabular benchmarks rather than large-scale transformer language models. In parallel, large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have demonstrated substantial reductions in per-token computation by activating only a small subset of experts for each input (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022). Recent work such as Mixture of a Million Experts (PEER) further pushes this paradigm by retrieving from extremely large pools of fine-grained experts, improving compute–performance trade-offs at scale (He, 2024). While effective, these approaches typically rely on separate routing networks, expert balancing mechanisms (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022), and specialized infrastructure (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Gale et al., 2023).

Another line of research focuses on contextual and activation-based sparsity. Methods such as Deja Vu predict at inference time which attention heads or MLP components are likely to be active/inactive for a given input, enabling conditional execution without retraining the model (Liu et al., 2023). Related approaches, including ShadowLLM, explore predictor-based mechanisms to dynamically prune attention and feed-forward computation (Akhauri et al., 2024). These techniques are effective for inference-time acceleration but generally operate on pretrained dense models and do not introduce sparsity during training or alter the feed-forward architecture itself.

Sparsity has also been explored through pruning and mask-based techniques. Structured and unstructured pruning methods aim to remove redundant parameters either during or after training, often inspired by the lottery ticket hypothesis and related frameworks (Hoefler et al., 2021). In addition, gated activation functions such as GLU and its variants (e.g., SwiGLU) have been widely adopted in transformer feed-forward blocks to improve expressivity and optimization stability (Shazeer, 2020). While these approaches improve performance, they do not significantly reduce computation, as all neurons remain active for every input.

Tree-based neural architectures and differentiable decision-tree layers have also been proposed as learnable components within neural networks (Thebelt et al., 2022). Such models combine tree structures with gradient-based optimization and have shown promising results in tabular and vision domains. Separately, transformer variants incorporating tree or syntactic structure as an inductive bias have been studied in representation learning and attention mechanisms (Wang et al., 2019). However, these approaches are typically not designed as drop-in replacements for dense feed-forward blocks in large-scale language models.

Compared to these prior approaches, tree-based feed-forward layers occupy a distinct design point. Rather than introducing separate expert routers, inference-time predictors, or post-hoc pruning, Fast Feedforward (FFF) layers integrate routing and computation within a single tree-structured feed-forward module. This enables extreme, input-dependent sparsity during both training and inference, with predictable and structured activation patterns. Prior work on FFF layers has been limited to relatively small models and restricted settings, leaving open questions regarding scalability, training stability, and performance in modern GPT-style large language models.

This work addresses these gaps by providing a systematic study of tree-based feed-forward layers as drop-in replacements for dense MLP blocks in large transformer architectures, evaluating their scalability, efficiency, and training dynamics under realistic large-scale training regimes.

3 Fast Feedforward Layer

Node parameterization.

An FFF layer (Belcák and Wattenhofer, 2023a) consists of PP trainable, perfect binary trees of depth DD, which are evaluated in parallel (see Fig. 1c). The computation proceeds sequentially through each tree root-to-leaf. Each node is indexed by a triple (p,ℓ,s)(p,\ell,s), where p∈{1,…,P}p\in\{1,\dots,P\} denotes the tree, ℓ∈{0,…,D}\ell\in\{0,\dots,D\} the level, and s∈{0,…,2ℓ−1}s\in\{0,\dots,2^{\ell}-1\} the position within the level. Each node (p,ℓ,s)(p,\ell,s) is associated with two sets of trainable parameters:

  • •

    Routing (linear_in): a weight vector wp,ℓ,sin∈ℝdinw^{\mathrm{in}}_{p,\ell,s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} and bias bp,ℓ,sin∈ℝb^{\mathrm{in}}_{p,\ell,s}\in\mathbb{R}, producing a single scalar logit;

  • •

    Output (linear_out): a weight vector wp,ℓ,sout∈ℝdoutw^{\mathrm{out}}_{p,\ell,s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}.

Forward computation.

For each input sample x∈ℝdinx\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} and each tree p∈{1,…,P}p\in\{1,\dots,P\}, traversal starts at the root s0=0s_{0}=0. For ℓ=0,…,D\ell=0,\dots,D, exactly one node is evaluated:

zp,ℓ​(x)=⟨x,wp,ℓ,sℓin⟩+bp,ℓ,sℓin∈ℝ.z_{p,\ell}(x)=\left\langle x,\;w^{\mathrm{in}}_{p,\ell,s_{\ell}}\right\rangle+b^{\mathrm{in}}_{p,\ell,s_{\ell}}\in\mathbb{R}. (1)

For ℓ=0,…,D−1\ell=0,\dots,D-1, the next node index is updated via a hard routing decision:

sℓ+1=2sℓ+[sg(zp,ℓ(x))≥0],s_{\ell+1}=2s_{\ell}+\mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathrm{sg}\!\left(z_{p,\ell}(x)\right)\geq 0\right], (2)

where 𝟏​(⋅)\mathbf{1}(\cdot) is the indicator function and sg⁡(⋅)\mathrm{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operator. Consequently, each tree requires a fixed number of DD routing steps and the layer has P×DP\times D active nodes in total. All active nodes contribute directly to the output, i.e. nodes on levels 0,…,D−10,\dots,D-1 have a double role of routing and output generation.

Sparse output computation.

The output y=FFF⁡(x)∈ℝdouty=\mathrm{FFF}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}} of the layer is obtained by summing the contributions of the visited nodes:

y=bout+∑p=1P∑ℓ=0DGELU⁡(zp,ℓ​(x))​wp,ℓ,sℓout.y=b^{\mathrm{out}}+\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{\ell=0}^{D}\mathrm{GELU}\!\left(z_{p,\ell}(x)\right)\;w^{\mathrm{out}}_{p,\ell,s_{\ell}}\;. (3)

4 Autoregressive Language Modeling

We train GPT-style language models with 125M parameters from scratch and compare dense feed-forward (FF) blocks, tree-based FFF layers, and sparsity-matched Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers under identical training pipelines (see Appendix H for details). We evaluate three FFF configurations with depth D=3,5,7D=3,5,7, corresponding to approximately 75%, 90%, and 97% sparsity. These models are compared against dense FF and MoEs with matched sparsity and top-k=2k=2 routing.

Figure 2 shows the training loss curves for all configurations. Results are averaged over three runs with different random seeds. FFF achieved performance comparable to sparsity-matched MoE baselines, with only negligible differences even at high sparsity of 97%. These results demonstrate that tree-based feed-forward layers can match the effectiveness of MoE at equivalent sparsity in small-scale models. Additional results in terms of perplexity (PPL) are reported in Appendix A.

5 Tree Utilization and Routing Imbalance

Expert utilization and routing balance are long-standing challenges in conditional computation models, particularly in mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures. Since the variant of FFF layers used here used no balancing mechanisms, we investigated whether similar utilization issues arise and how they manifest in practice.

We measured tree utilization by recording how frequently each path (or subtree) is visited during training and inference. Across different model sizes, tree depths, datasets, and tasks, we observe a consistent pattern of severe imbalance in tree utilization (Fig. 3). The distribution of branch visits is highly skewed: the leftmost path from the root is selected in more than 50%50\% of cases, while the left child of the right subtree accounts for over 15%15\% of visits. The remaining paths are activated only rarely (although we found only 1% ’dead’ leaf nodes, that were never visited, for d=3d=3 trees, 5% for d=5d=5 trees and 20% for d=7d=7 trees). This behavior mimics a heavy-tailed distribution over path utilization (see Appendix I for a discussion) and mirrors expert collapse observed in MoE models trained without balancing losses.

5.1 Architectural biases for balance / imbalance

In MoEs imbalance typically arises from learned routers, and can be accounted for by auxiliary balancing losses. However, since FFF has no dedictaed routing structure, the observed imbalance must stem from the interaction between the tree structure, the nonlinearity, and gradient-based training of the surrounding linear layers. In Appendix G we show through a detailed empirical and analytical investigation that this is in fact the case: the combination of hard binary routing and the GELU nonlinearity introduces an asymmetric gradient flow, where updates associated with negative node logits are strongly suppressed, while positive logits dominate the embedding space. This induces a systematic drift in node logits that biases routing decisions, to systemically prefer the left child (the child with lower index) over the right child, in every node.

Interestingly, our analysis also reveals that a simple change in architecture can fix this imbalance. This alternative design applies the nonlinearity after the sparse output accumulation:

FFFpost​(x)=GELU⁡(bout+∑p=1P∑ℓ=0Dzp,ℓ​(x)​wp,ℓ,sℓout).\mathrm{FFF}^{\mathrm{post}}(x)=\mathrm{GELU}\!\left(b^{\mathrm{out}}+\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{\ell=0}^{D}z_{p,\ell}(x)\;w^{\mathrm{out}}_{p,\ell,s_{\ell}}\right).

By adopting this post-GELU formulation, the gradient magnitude no longer directly depends on individual node logits. As a result, the sign-dependent gradient suppression responsible for imbalanced routing is no longer present. As shown analytically in Appendix G and empirically in Figure 3, this modification leads to substantially more balanced tree utilization across paths. Notably, this balancing mechanism does not rely on auxiliary losses, explicit load constraints, or router regularization, while maintaining all computational advantages of FFF.

5.2 Utilizing Imbalance: Auto-Pruning in Tree-Based Feed-Forward Layers

When we evaluated the balanced FFF version, we found to our surprise that task performance did not depend strongly on how balanced the trees were. In fact, our results presented in Appendix A show that the balanced FFF version even slightly underperformed the imbalanced version. This suggests the the sparse training used for FFF automatically leads to a competition for resources between tree paths and a uniform distribution of resources may not be the ideal strategy. We therefore wondered whether the observed imbalance could serve a computational advantage. As optimization progresses, certain paths of the tree become effectively and permanently inactive, resulting in a form of static structural sparsity on top of the input-dependent routing mechanism. This phenomenon manifests as a progressive concentration of computation on a subset of tree paths, while other paths receive diminishing gradient updates and eventually cease to contribute to the model output. Importantly, this auto-pruning behavior emerges automatically during training and arises from the interaction between hard tree routing decisions and the asymmetric nonlinearity of GELU, a combination that is specific to the proposed layer design.

Figure 4 illustrates the effect of path pruning on validation performance. We observe that, as training proceeds, models with increasing levels of permanent path deactivation can closely match the performance of their unpruned counterparts. This indicates that auto-pruning preserves the most informative computation paths while removing redundant ones. Overall, auto-pruning provides an additional source of efficiency by converting dynamic routing decisions into stable, data-dependent structural sparsity during training. While not the primary focus of this work, this effect helps explain the robustness and scalability of tree-based feed-forward layers observed in our experiments. In Appendix G we further evaluate the auto-pruning mechanism for the OPT 125M model, showing that pruning can be an effective mechanism to further sparsity deeper FFF layers.

6 Scaling Experiments

We have now developed the necessary tools to address the core goal of this work: to evaluate the scalability and practicality of the proposed Fast Feedforward (FFF) layer as an alternative to standard feed-forward blocks in large transformer models, that maintains high levels of sparsity during inference and training.

6.1 Language Modeling Setup

Model architecture.

We adopt a GPT-style transformer architecture for autoregressive language modeling (Zhang et al., 2022). In all experiments, the attention blocks remain structurally unchanged. We replace the conventional MLP layer following each attention block with the proposed FFF layer, using a hardware-compatible masked implementation (see Appendix F).

Training data and objective.

Models are trained using the standard next-token prediction objective on a large-scale language modeling corpus. Given a sequence of tokens (x1,…,xT)(x_{1},\dots,x_{T}), training minimizes the cross-entropy loss

ℒ=−∑t=1Tlogp(xt∣x<t).\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}). (4)

All models were trained with a ratio of ca. 20:120:1 for the number of training tokens to parameters, following (Hoffmann et al., 2022).

We consider two training regimes. In the first, models were trained entirely from scratch, with all parameters initialized randomly. In the second regime, which we refer to as fine-tuning (FT), attention layers and other trainable components were initialized from a pretrained dense model, while the feed-forward blocks were replaced by the proposed sparse routing layers, with random initial parameters. Although replacing even a single layer requires retraining the full model, this setup reflects a practical scenario in which a pretrained model is adapted by swapping in a sparse feed-forward component as a drop-in replacement.

To contextualize our results, we report performance for several pretrained reference models trained on substantially larger corpora. In particular, we include a pretrained OPT model trained on approximately 300B tokens (Zhang et al., 2022), as well as other publicly available models such as Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023) and TinyLLaMA (Zhang et al., 2024), which are trained on roughly 1T and 2T tokens, respectively. These models are provided for reference only and should not be considered direct baselines, as their training budgets far exceed those used in our experiments.

Our primary baselines are dense transformer models trained from scratch using the same architecture, optimization pipeline, and number of training tokens as our sparse models. This allows for a controlled comparison that isolates the effect of replacing the feed-forward layers. We report results for two main model sizes: a 125M-parameter model evaluated on language modeling and text generation tasks (see Section 4 and Appendix A), and a 1.3B-parameter model evaluated on both language modeling and downstream benchmarks. Additional results for larger models, including 2.7B and 6.7B parameters, are provided in the appendix. Technical details about implementation, optimization, and hyperparameters can be found in Appendix H.

6.2 Language Modeling Results

Training dynamics.

We evaluated FFF with depths 4 and 6, corresponding to approximately 83% and 94% sparsity, respectively, on a 1.3B-parameter OPT model. Depth 6 is selected based on the benchmark results in Section 7 as a favorable trade-off between sparsity and runtime efficiency, while depth 4 provides a more conservative sparsity setting. In addition to training from scratch, we also report fine-tuning results for both configurations, where attention layers are initialized from a pretrained dense model. Across all settings, the models with FFF layer maintain stable training dynamics and closely follow the dense feed-forward baseline (see Appendix B), indicating that highly sparse tree-based routing layers can be trained reliably and integrated into large language models under both training regimes.

Evaluation on held-out data.

For quantitative evaluation, we report perplexity on a standard held-out language modeling benchmark. Perplexity (Fang et al., 2024) is defined as

PPL=exp(1T∑t=1T−logp(xt∣x<t)).\mathrm{PPL}=\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}-\log p(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\right). (5)

As shown in Table 1, FFF models at 1.3B parameter scales achieve perplexities comparable to their dense baselines. Performance differences are typically within 10%10\%, indicating that tree-based sparsification does not substantially degrade language modeling quality.

6.3 Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Evaluation

To assess generalization beyond the training distribution, we evaluate models on a diverse suite of downstream language understanding tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. We report both zero-shot and few-shot accuracy across multiple benchmarks, to reduce the impact of task-specific variance or chance.

Tables 2 and 3 summarizes zero-shot and few-shot performance. Across most tasks, FFF closely matches or exceeds the performance of dense feed-forward baselines when trained or fine-tuned on the same amount of data. In several cases, the tree-based variants outperform the dense model despite operating in significantly higher sparsity regimes.

We additionally include a pretrained OPT model trained on approximately 300B tokens as a reference point. Due to its substantially larger training budget compared to our models (trained on roughly 26B tokens), this model performs better on some tasks that benefit from broader topic coverage — such as Obqa. Nevertheless, on multiple benchmarks (see e.g. ARC-e) all FFF layer configurations, including highly sparse variants, outperform the pretrained OPT model. Similar trends are observed across other tasks, where fine-tuned FFF models consistently achieve equal or higher accuracy than their dense counterparts.

Notably, results on MMLU (Table 3), reported as an average across all subtasks, show that sparser FFF models can achieve higher accuracy than dense feed-forward baselines. These findings indicate that tree-based sparse routing not only scales effectively to large language models, but can also preserve, and in some cases improve, generalization and in-context learning performance, even under extreme sparsity and reduced training data.

Beyond training from scratch and fine-tuning in language models.

We also evaluated the proposed sparse routing layer in additional settings to further assess its applicability. In particular, we applied FFF to a transformer-based object detection model (DETR), showing that the sparse layers match the performance of their dense counterparts and exhibit stable training behavior. Detailed results are reported in the Appendix D In Appendix C, we present additional results for 2.7B and 6.7B parameter OPT models showing promising results for the d=4d=4 FFF variant.

7 Efficiency of Tree-Based Feed-Forward Layers

Efficiency in terms of both runtime and computational cost is a central motivation for introducing tree-based feed-forward layers in large-scale models. While the Fast Feedforward (FFF) layer enables high structured sparsity, it also introduces a sequential, depth-wise execution pattern that differs fundamentally from the fully parallel execution of dense feed-forward blocks. This raises an important practical question: can such a highly sparse but hierarchical layer be computationally competitive, or even advantageous, at scale?

To address this question, we benchmark the execution of FFF under its intended sparse computation model and compare it against a dense feed-forward baseline. Rather than focusing on kernel-level optimizations on current accelerators, our goal is to evaluate whether the substantial reduction in computation enabled by tree-based sparsity can outweigh the overhead of sequential traversal.

7.1 Runtime Speedup

We evaluate the runtime behavior of tree-based feed-forward layers under their sequential sparse execution model, in which only the nodes along the active traversal path are evaluated and all inactive paths incur no computation. Runtime is measured at the layer level and compared against a dense feed-forward baseline under identical conditions.

As shown in Fig. 5 and summarized in Table 5, increasing tree depth leads to substantial runtime improvements despite the introduction of depth-wise sequential traversal. For configurations relevant to large language models, a tree depth of 6 achieves the highest speedup, with an average improvement of approximately 8.7×8.7\times over dense feed-forward layers. While deeper trees further reduce computation, diminishing returns and increased traversal overhead limit additional gains.

These results identify depth 6 as a practical trade-off between extreme sparsity and efficient execution. We therefore adopt this configuration in most of our large-scale experiments, alongside shallower settings that prioritize reduced routing depth.

7.2 Sparsity and FLOPs Analysis

We characterize sparsity and computational cost at both the layer and model levels. Feed-forward layer sparsity measures the fraction of inactive nodes within the tree-based feed-forward layers and isolates the sparsity induced by the proposed architecture. Effective model sparsity captures the resulting reduction in computation across the full transformer, accounting for the fact that attention layers remain dense.

As summarized in Table 4, sparsity grows exponentially with tree depth. Even shallow configurations achieve high sparsity (e.g., approximately 83% for d=4d=4), while deeper trees reach extreme regimes, exceeding 94% sparsity at depth 6 and more than 99% at depth 13. This behavior follows directly from the hierarchical structure of the trees and the activation of a single path per input.

To complement the runtime measurements, we also report analytical estimates of per-token floating-point operations (FLOPs), computed based on the number of activated nodes along each routing path. Table 4 reports FLOPs normalized to a dense feed-forward baseline and confirms an exponential reduction with increasing tree depth, consistent with the observed sparsity trends.

While total FLOPs decrease sharply with increasing sparsity, measured throughput in terms of FLOPs per second also decreases. This behavior is expected and desirable: as the amount of computation performed per token is reduced, the aggregate FLOPs executed per second naturally drop. In this regime, FLOPs/s reflects the reduced computational demand rather than a slowdown of the layer itself, as demonstrated by the measured speedups, where wall-clock runtime improves despite the lower FLOPs/s.

8 Discussion

In this work, we studied tree-based sparse feed-forward layers as structured alternatives to dense feed-forward (FF) layers, demonstrating that they perform on par with mixture-of-experts models. This indicates that tree-based routing can serve as a practical, scalable, and predictable sparsification mechanism. We demonstrated that replacing dense FF layers with tree-based sparse layers scales effectively to large language models and generalizes across tasks and domains while maintaining performance close to dense baselines.

Across multiple model sizes and evaluation settings, we showed that these layers can operate in high sparsity regimes—often exceeding 90%—while achieving comparable and, in several cases, superior performance relative to dense FF baselines trained under the same data and optimization budgets. Notably, we observed that sparse tree-based models can outperform dense counterparts despite activating only a small fraction of parameters, highlighting the effectiveness of structured, input-dependent computation.

Beyond empirical performance, we analyzed the routing dynamics induced by hierarchical binary trees and identified an emergent auto-pruning behavior. This mechanism converts dynamic, input-dependent routing into stable structural sparsity, enabling permanent deactivation of redundant computation paths without auxiliary losses or explicit pruning criteria. We further showed that routing imbalance—often viewed as a limitation in sparse architectures—is not necessarily harmful in tree-based routing and can be controlled through simple architectural choices when needed.

While our results indicate strong potential for both scalability and efficiency, we note that the practical runtime benefits of such layers are currently constrained by hardware and software support. Many highly optimized components in large language models rely on accelerator-specific kernels, whereas dynamic, tree-based sparse execution remains underexplored in current hardware stacks. As such, our efficiency results are intended to highlight theoretical and simulated potential rather than immediate deployment-ready speedups.

Overall, this work aims to encourage further exploration of tree-based sparse computation as a viable direction for efficient large-scale models. We believe that the combination of dynamic, predictable, and structured sparsity, along with emerging auto-pruning properties, makes tree-based feed-forward layers a promising foundation for future research in scalable and efficient neural architectures.

Impact Statement

This work aims to advance the field of machine learning by studying structured sparse feed-forward layers for modern transformer architectures. From an ethical perspective, the proposed tree-based design introduces a more structured and interpretable form of conditional computation, which may help improve understanding and transparency of model behavior compared to fully dense architectures.

From a societal standpoint, large transformer models are computationally and energy intensive. By enabling extreme and dynamic sparsity while preserving performance, this work contributes toward more computationally efficient model designs, which may help reduce energy consumption and environmental impact during training and deployment at scale. While the work does not directly address downstream applications or deployment risks, it encourages future research on efficient, scalable, and responsible large-scale machine learning systems.

Appendix A Additional Perplexity Results

This appendix provides additional evaluation results. Table 6 reports perplexity (PPL) values for various OPT-125M parameter model configurations trained from scratch.

Appendix B Training Dynamics for the 1.3B Model

This appendix presents training loss curves for the 1.3B-parameter language model to complement the evaluation results reported in the main text. While quantitative metrics for this model size are discussed in Section 6, the plots here provide additional insight into optimization stability and training behavior.

Figure 6 shows two training regimes. The left panel reports training from scratch for three configurations: a dense feed-forward (FF) baseline and two Fast Feedforward (FFF) variants with tree depths 4 and 6. All models are trained using the same pipeline and budget. The curves demonstrate that both FFF configurations closely track the dense baseline throughout training, indicating stable optimization even at high sparsity levels.

The right panel shows the fine-tuning regime, where the dense FF layers of a pretrained OPT-1.3B model are replaced with FFF layers, while all remaining weights are initialized from the pretrained checkpoint. Training remains stable, and the loss rapidly converges to the expected range, demonstrating that FFF layers can be integrated into pretrained large language models and adapted efficiently through fine-tuning.

Appendix C Additional Large-Scale Training Results

To further evaluate the scalability of tree-based feed-forward layers, we conduct additional training experiments on larger OPT-style models with 2.7B and 6.7B parameters. Due to computational constraints, these models are trained from scratch in a controlled environment using a reduced subset of the SlimPajama dataset (Soboleva et al., 2023). As a result, these experiments are not intended to provide a direct comparison with the models trained on the full dataset, but rather to assess training stability and scaling behavior.

For each model size, we compare a dense feed-forward baseline with a Forest Router configuration of depth 4, corresponding to approximately 84% sparsity. Both models are trained using the same architecture, optimization pipeline, and data subset. Each plot reports two runs, one for the dense feed-forward model and one for FFF.

As shown in Fig. 7, FFF models closely follow the training dynamics of dense feed-forward baselines. In both model sizes, the sparse models exhibit comparable or slightly improved loss trajectories during the early and middle stages of training. While we cannot verify whether this advantage would persist through full training on a substantially larger dataset, similar behavior has been observed in smaller models, where dense feed-forward layers ultimately achieve marginally lower final loss. Nevertheless, the small performance gap and stable optimization behavior indicate that FFF layers remain a viable replacement at these scales.

Overall, these results provide additional evidence that tree-based feed-forward layers can be scaled to multi-billion-parameter models while maintaining stable training dynamics and competitive performance.

Appendix D Extension to Vision Tasks

To evaluate whether tree-based feed-forward layers generalize beyond language modeling, we apply the same replacement strategy to a transformer-based object detection model. Specifically, we replace the feed-forward layers in a DETR architecture (Carion et al., 2020) with Fast Feedforward (FFF) layers, while keeping all other components unchanged.

We train both the dense FF baseline and the FFF-based DETR model under a fixed compute budget, using the CPPE-5 dataset (Dagli and Shaikh, 2023) for object detection. Training is performed for a fixed number of epochs due to computational constraints. All experiments are repeated over multiple runs with different random seeds, and results are reported as averages to reduce variance.

Figure 8 summarizes the results. The left panel shows the training loss curves, while the right panel reports evaluation performance measured by mAP​@​50\mathrm{mAP}@50, i.e., mean Average Precision computed at an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5, a standard metric for object detection. Across runs, the FFF-based model closely matches the performance of the dense feed-forward baseline, and in some cases slightly outperforms it.

Due to limited compute, we do not compare against long-horizon training or fully pretrained DETR models. Nevertheless, these results indicate that FFF layers can serve as effective drop-in replacements for dense feed-forward blocks in vision transformers, extending the applicability of tree-based sparse computation beyond language models.

Appendix E CDF–PDF relation and monotonicity of p=ℙ⁡(z>0)p=\mathbb{P}(z>0)

Let z∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) with σ>0\sigma>0 and define p=ℙ⁡(z>0)p=\mathbb{P}(z>0). Standardize z~=(z−μ)/σ∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\tilde{z}=(z-\mu)/\sigma\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1):

p=ℙ⁡(z>0)=ℙ⁡(z~>−μσ)=1−Φ⁡(−μσ)=Φ⁡(μσ),p=\mathbb{P}(z>0)=\mathbb{P}\!\left(\tilde{z}>\frac{-\mu}{\sigma}\right)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{-\mu}{\sigma}\right)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\right), (6)

where Φ\Phi is the CDF of the standard normal distribution.

CDF and PDF.

For any continuous random variable, the CDF is the integral of its PDF:

Φ⁡(x)=∫−∞xϕ⁡(t)​𝑑t,⇒dd​x​Φ​(x)=ϕ⁡(x).\Phi(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}\phi(t)\,dt,\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\frac{d}{dx}\Phi(x)=\phi(x). (7)

For the standard normal,

ϕ⁡(x)=12​π​exp⁡(−x22)>0for all ​x∈ℝ.\phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)>0\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}. (8)

Using the chain rule,

∂p∂μ=∂∂μ​Φ​(μσ)=ϕ⁡(μσ)⋅1σ.\frac{\partial p}{\partial\mu}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu}\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\right)=\phi\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\right)\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma}. (9)

Since σ>0\sigma>0 and ϕ⁡(⋅)>0\phi(\cdot)>0, we obtain ∂p∂μ>0\frac{\partial p}{\partial\mu}>0, hence pp increases monotonically with μ\mu.

Appendix F FFF Block: Forward and Backward

To simplify the theoretical analysis and implementation for the large-scale experiments, we use a masked implementation of the FFF layer that is fully compatible with existing GPU kernels. This formulation is functionally equivalent to the sequential tree traversal described in the main text: it produces identical forward activations and backward gradients for all parameters.

FFF layer.

Let X∈ℝB×dinX\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} with BB and dind_{\mathrm{in}} representing the batch size and input dimensionality, respectively. We project to per-tree node logits

Z=reshape⁡(X​Win+𝐛in)∈ℝB×P×N,Z=\mathrm{reshape}(XW_{\mathrm{in}}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{in}})\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times P\times N}, (10)

where PP and NN refer to the number of parallel trees and nodes per tree, respectively. We define a stop-gradient operator sg⁡(⋅)\mathrm{sg}(\cdot) such that ∂sg⁡(u)∂u=0\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{sg}(u)}{\partial u}=0 and sg⁡(u)=u\mathrm{sg}(u)=u in the forward pass. The tree routing process, i.e. traversing the tree level by level and choosing a node based on the previous layer’s node output, is represented by the binary-tree search (BTS) operator. It produces a binary mask

M=BTS⁡(sg⁡(Z))∈{0,1}B×P×N,M=\mathrm{BTS}(\mathrm{sg}(Z))\in\{0,1\}^{B\times P\times N}, (11)

that can be multiplied element-wise with ZZ to select the outputs from the active nodes. Note that ZZ is computed directly from the input for all nodes and afterwards BTS realizes the tree structure by selecting an active path down the tree. Conceptually, BTS can be considered a specific form of expert selection module that shares its parameters with the experts represented by individual tree paths. This view on FFF is functionally identical to the formulation in the main text, but greatly simplifies the theoretical analysis presented here. Additionally, experts share some of their parameters where ever the corresponding paths overlap.

To produce the FFF block’s output, we apply the nonlinearity and then mask:

G=GELU⁡(Z),A=M⊙G.G=\mathrm{GELU}(Z),\qquad A=M\odot G. (12)

Flattening across (P,N)(P,N) yields A¯=flatten⁡(A)∈ℝB×(P​N)\bar{A}=\mathrm{flatten}(A)\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times(PN)}, and the layer output is

Y=A¯​Wout+𝐛out.Y=\bar{A}W_{\mathrm{out}}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{out}}. (13)

Equivalently with omitting the reshape operations for simplicity,

FFF⁡(X)=linear​_​out​(BTS⁡(sg⁡(Z))⊙GELU⁡(Z)),Z=linear​_​in​(X).\mathrm{FFF}(X)=\mathrm{linear\_out}\!\left(\mathrm{BTS}(\mathrm{sg}(Z))\odot\mathrm{GELU}(Z)\right),\quad Z=\mathrm{linear\_in}(X). (14)

Backward pass (no gradients through BTS).

Let ▽Y=∂ℒ∂Y\triangledown_{Y}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial Y}. Backprop through the output projection gives

▽A¯=▽Y​Wout⊤,∂ℒ∂Wout=A¯⊤​▽Y,∂ℒ∂𝐛out=∑b=1B▽Y,b.\triangledown_{\bar{A}}=\triangledown_{Y}W_{\mathrm{out}}^{\top},\quad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W_{\mathrm{out}}}=\bar{A}^{\top}\triangledown_{Y},\quad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{out}}}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\triangledown_{Y,b}. (15)

Unflatten ▽A¯\triangledown_{\bar{A}} to ▽A∈ℝB×P×N\triangledown_{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times P\times N}. Since A=M⊙GA=M\odot G and M=BTS⁡(sg⁡(Z))M=\mathrm{BTS}(\mathrm{sg}(Z)), we enforce ∂M∂Z=0\frac{\partial M}{\partial Z}=0, hence

▽Z≡∂ℒ∂Z=M⊙▽A.\triangledown_{Z}\equiv\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial Z}=M\odot\triangledown_{A}. (26)

Flatten ▽Z\triangledown_{Z} to ▽flat=flatten⁡(▽Z)∈ℝB×(P​N)\triangledown_{\mathrm{flat}}=\mathrm{flatten}(\triangledown_{Z})\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times(PN)}. Then

∂ℒ∂Win=X⊤​▽flat,∂ℒ∂𝐛in=∑b=1B▽flat,b,∂ℒ∂X=▽flat​Win⊤.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W_{\mathrm{in}}}=X^{\top}\triangledown_{\mathrm{flat}},\quad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{in}}}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\triangledown_{\mathrm{flat},b},\quad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial X}=\triangledown_{\mathrm{flat}}W_{\mathrm{in}}^{\top}. (27)

Positive-branch probability under Gaussian logits.

Assuming the node logit follows z∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), the probability of selecting the positive branch is

p≜ℙ⁡(z>0)=Φ⁡(μσ),p\triangleq\mathbb{P}(z>0)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\right), (28)

where Φ\Phi is the standard normal CDF. Consequently pp is monotonically increasing in the mean μ\mu (see Appendix E).

Mean-logit drift under masked GELU gating.

Consider one node logit z=w⊤​h+bz=w^{\top}h+b produced inside linear​_​in\mathrm{linear\_in}. Define the mean logit μ≜𝔼⁡[z]=w⊤​m+b\mu\triangleq\mathbb{E}[z]=w^{\top}m+b where m=𝔼⁡[h]m=\mathbb{E}[h]. Under SGD,

w+=w−η​∂ℒ∂w,b+=b−η​∂ℒ∂b,w^{+}=w-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial w},\qquad b^{+}=b-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial b}, (29)

hence

μ+−μ=(w+−w)⊤​m+(b+−b)=−η⁡(m⊤​∂ℒ∂w+∂ℒ∂b).\mu^{+}-\mu=(w^{+}-w)^{\top}m+(b^{+}-b)=-\eta\left(m^{\top}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial w}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial b}\right). (30)

Using ∂ℒ∂w=∂ℒ∂z​h\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial w}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z}\,h and ∂ℒ∂b=∂ℒ∂z\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial b}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z} gives

𝔼⁡[μ+−μ]=−η​𝔼​[(∂ℒ∂z)​(m⊤​h+1)].\mathbb{E}[\mu^{+}-\mu]=-\eta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z}\right)(m^{\top}h+1)\right]. (31)

For the FFF variant Y=linear​_​out​(M⊙GELU⁡(Z))Y=\mathrm{linear\_out}(M\odot\mathrm{GELU}(Z)), we treat M=BTS⁡(sg⁡(Z))M=\mathrm{BTS}(\mathrm{sg}(Z)) as constant in backprop, i.e. ∂M/∂Z=0\partial M/\partial Z=0. Let g≜∂ℒ/∂(M​GELU​(z))g\triangleq\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial(M\,\mathrm{GELU}(z)) be the upstream gradient at this node. Then

∂ℒ∂z=g⋅M⋅GELU′​(z),\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z}=g\cdot M\cdot\mathrm{GELU}^{\prime}(z), (32)

and therefore

𝔼⁡[μ+−μ]=−η​𝔼​[g​M​GELU′​(z)​(m⊤​h+1)].\mathbb{E}[\mu^{+}-\mu]=-\eta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[g\,M\,\mathrm{GELU}^{\prime}(z)\,(m^{\top}h+1)\right]. (33)

Splitting over z>0z>0 and z<0z<0 yields two contributions. Since GELU′​(z)\mathrm{GELU}^{\prime}(z) is close to 11 for z>0z>0 and substantially smaller for z<0z<0, the negative-side term is typically suppressed, giving the approximation

𝔼⁡[μ+−μ]≈−η​𝔼​[g​M​(m⊤​h+1)∣z>0]​ℙ​(z>0).\mathbb{E}[\mu^{+}-\mu]\approx-\eta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[g\,M\,(m^{\top}h+1)\mid z>0\right]\mathbb{P}(z>0). (34)

Empirically we observe the upstream signal gg has negative mean during training (Appendix G), which makes the right-hand side positive (under mild regularity/weak-correlation assumptions), implying 𝔼⁡[μ+−μ]>0\mathbb{E}[\mu^{+}-\mu]>0. Since p=ℙ⁡(z>0)=Φ⁡(μ/σ)p=\mathbb{P}(z>0)=\Phi(\mu/\sigma) and ∂p/∂μ>0\partial p/\partial\mu>0 (Appendix E), this corresponds to 𝔼⁡[Δ​p]>0\mathbb{E}[\Delta p]>0.

Appendix G Auto-Pruning Analysis

This appendix provides a detailed empirical and analytical investigation of the auto-pruning behavior observed in tree-based feed-forward layers. For simplicity, the analysis is presented using the masked formulation of the FFF layer, which is functionally equivalent to the sequential tree traversal described in the main text. We show how stable structural sparsity emerges from the interaction between hard tree routing decisions and the asymmetric nonlinearity of GELU.

G.1 Empirical Observations

To isolate the underlying dynamics of auto-pruning, we conduct controlled toy experiments using a large batch size of 10,000 to minimize stochastic effects during training.

The first observation concerns the distribution of activations at a randomly selected internal tree node. As shown in Fig. 9 (right), the node logit follows an approximately zero-mean normal distribution after training. This symmetry indicates that routing decisions are not biased toward either branch at initialization and that specialization arises through training dynamics.

The second observation analyzes the gradient signal received by the same node during backpropagation. Fig. 9 (left) shows the distribution of the upstream gradient after an initial transient phase. We observe that the gradient concentrates almost entirely in the negative regime. This persistent negative signal encourages the routing gate to suppress one branch consistently, driving the node toward permanent deactivation due to the combination of GELU as an asymmetric nonlinearity and the hard thresholding of the tree.

Together, these observations provide empirical evidence that motivates the analysis of the auto-pruning dynamics and mechanisms presented in the next section.

G.2 Analytical Explanation

Consider the routing logit for a single tree node,

z=w⊤​h+b,z=w^{\top}h+b, (35)

where hh denotes the node input and w,bw,b are the parameters of the routing projection. We define the mean logit as

μ≜𝔼⁡[z].\mu\triangleq\mathbb{E}[z]. (36)

Empirically, we observe that zz remains approximately Gaussian across training,

z∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2),z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), (37)

which motivates the following analysis.

The probability of selecting the positive branch is

p=ℙ⁡(z>0)=Φ⁡(μσ),p=\mathbb{P}(z>0)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\right), (38)

where Φ\Phi denotes the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Since Φ\Phi is monotonic, any positive drift in μ\mu increases the likelihood of selecting the same branch.

During training with stochastic gradient descent, the expected change in the mean logit satisfies

𝔼⁡[Δ​μ]=−η​𝔼​[∂ℒ∂z​(m⊤​h+1)],m≜𝔼⁡[h],\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu]=-\eta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z}(m^{\top}h+1)\right],\quad m\triangleq\mathbb{E}[h], (39)

where η\eta is the learning rate and ℒ\mathcal{L} the task loss.

For the standard FFF formulation,

Y=linear​_​out​(M⊙GELU⁡(Z)),Y=\mathrm{linear\_out}(M\odot\mathrm{GELU}(Z)), (40)

the routing mask M=BTS⁡(sg⁡(Z))M=\mathrm{BTS}(\mathrm{sg}(Z)) is treated as constant during backpropagation. Let

g≜∂ℒ∂(M​GELU​(z))g\triangleq\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(M\,\mathrm{GELU}(z))} (41)

denote the upstream gradient. The gradient with respect to zz becomes

∂ℒ∂z=g⋅M⋅GELU′​(z).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z}=g\cdot M\cdot\mathrm{GELU}^{\prime}(z). (42)

Since GELU′​(z)\mathrm{GELU}^{\prime}(z) is close to 11 for z>0z>0 and significantly smaller for z<0z<0, gradient contributions from the negative region are suppressed. Empirically, we observe that the upstream gradient gg has a negative mean, yielding

𝔼⁡[Δ​μ]>0,\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu]>0, (43)

which causes μ\mu to drift toward positive values. This reinforces the selection of the same branch and progressively suppresses alternatives.

G.3 From Dynamic Routing to Static Sparsity

As training progresses, nodes whose logits consistently drift negative are visited increasingly rarely. These nodes receive diminishing gradient updates and eventually become permanently inactive, leading to the deactivation of entire subtrees. This process converts dynamic, input-dependent routing into stable, data-dependent structural sparsity.

Figure 4 illustrates this effect by evaluating validation accuracy under fixed statistical pruning ratios. As training proceeds, models with increasing levels of permanent pruning closely match the performance of their unpruned counterparts, indicating that auto-pruning preserves the most informative computation paths.

G.4 Effect of Nonlinearity Placement

For the alternative FFFpost\mathrm{FFF}^{\mathrm{post}} formulation,

Y=GELU⁡(linear​_​out​(M⊙Z)),Y=\mathrm{GELU}(\mathrm{linear\_out}(M\odot Z)), (44)

the gradient with respect to zz no longer depends directly on GELU′​(z)\mathrm{GELU}^{\prime}(z), but on a mixed representation after aggregation. As a result, the sign-dependent suppression mechanism described above is absent, and we do not observe stable auto-pruning behavior empirically. This effect instead leads to a more balanced tree utilization, as discussed and tested in Section 3.

G.5 Pruning results for LLMs

In Fig. 10 we evaluate the impact of static sparsity on the OPT 125M model. We removed the fractions of least used tree nodes effectively, pruning the model after training. As expected, pruning had higher impact on FFFpost{}^{\text{post}} variant than on FFF. Moreover, pruning was more effective on deeper trees, FFF layers with d=7d=7 could be pruned by up to 40% without significant drop in task performance, but perplexity was overall higher for sparser models.

G.6 Summary

Together, these results show that auto-pruning arises from a specific interaction between hard binary routing and the asymmetric GELU nonlinearity in the pre-activation design. This mechanism naturally transforms dynamic routing into stable structural sparsity during training, without explicit pruning rules or auxiliary losses.

Appendix H Implementation and Training Details

All experiments were conducted on a multi-node GPU cluster equipped with NVIDIA A100 GPUs. For the OPT-125M experiments, we used multi compute nodes, each containing 4 GPUs. Training was implemented using the Hugging Face Transformers framework with DeepSpeed integration and the Accelerate library for distributed execution and mixed-precision training.

We followed a Chinchilla-style training paradigm, where training proceeds for a single epoch while controlling the total number of tokens processed rather than training to convergence over multiple epochs. The total number of tokens per optimization step was fixed to approximately 5×1055\times 10^{5} tokens for 125 million paramter model , 1×1061\times 10^{6} tokens for 1 billion parameter model, and 2×1062\times 10^{6} tokens for 3 and 7 billion paramter model. Per-device batch size and gradient accumulation steps were chosen accordingly to reach this target token budget across all GPUs.

Optimization was performed using AdamW with fused CUDA kernels, cosine learning rate scheduling with a linear warmup phase, and gradient clipping with a maximum norm of 1.0. Training was conducted in FP16 precision. No maximum number of steps was imposed, and training was terminated after completing one full pass over the dataset.

For simplicity, the analysis is presented using the masked formulation of the FFF layer, which is functionally equivalent to the sequential tree traversal version described in the main text.

Dataset

The SlimPajama (Soboleva et al., 2023) dataset was used for training. The dataset was tokenized offline prior to training using a GPT-style tokenizer. Tokenized shards were randomly sampled across runs using a fixed random seed to ensure reproducibility while maintaining stochasticity in shard selection. All tokenization and sharding were performed before training to eliminate runtime preprocessing overhead.

H.1 Hyperparameters

Table 7 summarizes the hyperparameters and training configuration used for the OPT-125M experiments. Unless stated otherwise, all values were kept fixed across runs for this model size. Method-specific architectural details are described in the main paper, while this appendix focuses on reproducibility-relevant training and optimization settings.

Appendix I Inductive Biases for Heavy-Tailed Distributions in Binary Trees

It can be easily seen that a binary tree can be constructed to realize any distribution over paths. This can be done by starting with any target distribution, assigning this to leaves, re-normalizing, and iteratively summing probabilities of child nodes until the root is reached. Figure  11 illustrates this. 4 different binary trees with d=5d=5 are shown, a uniform distribution, an approximate heavy tailed distribution with finite support and the same heavy tailed distribution with re-ordered leaves (indices ordered breadth first instead of depth first). The heavy tailed distributions are given here by Pareto distributions with α=2.0\alpha=2.0. Branch weights are indicated by color and labels for first 2 levels. The bottom right tree is generated based on the mean path utilization from our imbalanced model as in Fig. 3. It can be clearly seen that the branch weights are more similar to the heavy tailed model (bottom left), and that this model is best compatible with the imbalanced tree structure (left child preferred over right). Heavy-tailed distributions have been identified as a powerful inductive bias that could be responsible for some of the emergent properties of LLMs (Chan et al., 2022). Our results suggest that FFFs have an inductive bias built in, that skews path utilization to mimic such heavy tailed distributions.

Appendix J Visualization of Space Partitioning

To illustrate the structured behavior of tree-based routing, we analyze an FFF layer on a simple 2D toy task. The input is a point (x1,x2)∈ℝ2(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and the target is a binary label defined by a checkered-field (checkerboard) pattern over the input space. This setting allows us to directly visualize how hierarchical routing partitions the input domain.

Figure 12 provides two complementary views of the learned partitioning. The left panel visualizes the decision boundaries induced by tree traversal, mapped back into the original input space. Each line corresponds to a routing split at some node, and together the boundaries show how the forest decomposes the 2D plane into a collection of routed regions. The right panel visualizes the resulting routed regions in representation space: we group inputs by their routing outcome (i.e., the set of active paths) and project the corresponding representations using PCA. Regions are color-coded, highlighting that different parts of the input space are consistently assigned to different routing patterns that contribute differently to the final output.

The first meaning is a negative one, because we know that after you
